quote: He called it an a-machine, for automatic machine
problem: In p4's last sentence, 'it' means the decider ("so it cannot exist"), so a reader first links 'a-machine' and the bold 'Turing machine' to the impossible decider. They have to re-read back to p4's second sentence to find that 'it' means the imagined device (tape, head, rules).
fix: name the noun: 'He called his imagined device an a-machine'
reason: p4 ends on the decider ('so it cannot exist, and neither can Hilbert's procedure'), and p5 opens 'He called it an a-machine'. Nearest antecedents are the decider, Hilbert's procedure and 'this program'. The device was named several sentences earlier, so the bold 'Turing machine' can attach to the wrong thing. Cheap fix, low severity.
judge_fix: In ch1-context-p5 change the first sentence to: 'He called the device an _a-machine_, for automatic machine; we now call it a **Turing machine**.'

quote: A positive voltage on the gate pulls electrons up under the oxide
problem: The p7 repair holds in the prose: the gate draws free electrons out of the n-type source and drain, and p-type silicon has holes, not free electrons. The figure undoes it. In the drawing (frames t0, t2.667, t5.333), about nine free electrons sit loose in the middle of the p-type body at 0 V and rise straight up into the channel when the gate turns on. The caption and picture description say 'pulls electrons up', and the junction barrier p7 describes is not drawn. So the reader meets two answers to 'where do the electrons come from?' and cannot tell which is right.
fix: redraw Fig 1.5: p-type body nearly empty at 0 V, channel filling sideways from source and drain; caption 'draws electrons in from the source and drain under the oxide'
reason: Verified in the SVG and the screenshots (fig-1-5 t0, t2.667, t5.333). At 0 V about nine loose electrons float in the middle of the p-type body. With + voltage they rise straight up into the channel, while the n-type source and drain hold only one or two dots each. This contradicts p7 ('draws free electrons out of the source and drain') and the strip ('the source and drain are n-type, rich in free electrons'). It also shows free electrons in p-type silicon, which has holes. The caption ('pulls electrons up') and the SVG <desc> repeat the wrong picture. Fig 1.5 is not a kept-original figure, so it can be fixed.
judge_fix: Figure: at 0 V draw no loose dots in the p-body; put the electron dots inside the two n-type regions. When the gate goes positive, animate those dots sliding out of the source and drain along the surface into the channel under the oxide, then back at 0 V. Caption (ch1-transistor-p8): 'A positive voltage on the gate draws electrons in from the source and drain until they form a thin channel under the oxide between them, and current flows.' Keep the balloon sentence. Update the <desc> to match: 'draws electrons in from the source and drain into a thin channel under it'. Strip item 3 can stay.

quote: or leave a file's pages unread until needed
problem: Nothing so far says that a file (for example the program's own instructions on disk) can sit in a program's virtual memory as pages, so the reader cannot tell which file is meant or why it would have pages in memory.
fix: say which file, and that its pages join the program's memory but are read from disk only when first touched
reason: The clause 'leave a file's pages unread until needed' brings in an idea no earlier text introduced, a file whose pages sit in a program's memory. It does not say which file. The reader cannot tell why a file would have pages in memory at all. The next clause explains the page-fault mechanism but not which file or why. Low severity, one short clause.
judge_fix: In ch1-memory-p10 replace 'or leave a file's pages unread until needed' with 'or read a program's file in from disk only as its pages are first used'.

quote: pass the MMU's checks, because they write only into the program's own writable memory
problem: p10 has just said the MMU enforces execute permission, yet the attack runs instructions placed in a data buffer, and the reader cannot see why that execute step gets past the MMU (DEP is only named).
fix: one clause: the stack used to be marked executable, and DEP is the defence that marks it not
reason: p10 has just said the page tables encode execute permission and the MMU enforces it. p11 opens by saying the attack passes the MMU's checks, then has the attacker fill the buffer with instructions and aim the return address at them, which is an execute from a data page. As written, p10 contradicts the attack. The missing premise is that the stack used to be executable, which is what DEP changes. The strip only names DEP in a list. The classic attack needs an executable stack (or a trick around DEP).
judge_fix: In ch1-memory-p11 after '...aim the return address at them.' add: 'That runs only where the stack is marked executable, and the MMU allows it unless DEP marks it not.' Then keep the last sentence ('Chapter 3 shows the defences...'). If the first sentence needs tightening: 'pass the MMU's write checks, because they write only into the program's own writable memory.'

quote: It filled a room thirty metres long, weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts
problem: Thirty metres (100 ft) is the length of ENIAC's cabinets laid end to end, not the length of the room. The machine stood in a U along the walls of a room 30 by 50 feet, about 9 by 15 metres.
fix: "Its cabinets, nearly thirty metres of them, lined a room fifteen metres long; it weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts, and broke down..." Sources: IEEE Milestone, ethw.org/Milestones:Electronic_Numerical_Integrator_and_Computer,_1946 ("almost one hundred feet long", "filled a 30-by-50 foot room"); pbs.org/transistor/science/events/eniac.html ("Filling up a 30 X 50 foot room").
reason: Checked ethw.org IEEE Milestone: machine 'almost one hundred feet long', room about 30 by 50 ft (about 9 by 15 m). Thirty metres is the cabinet run, not the room. Real factual slip in the book's opening hardware example.
judge_fix: ch1-transistor-p1: "It stretched thirty metres in cabinets, set in a U around a room fifteen metres long, weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts, and broke down on average every two days because a tube would burn out." Source: ethw.org/Milestones:Electronic_Numerical_Integrator_and_Computer,_1946.

quote: ENIAC filled a thirty-metre hall with 17,468 vacuum tubes
problem: This is the same room-versus-machine mix-up as in p1. The drawing makes it worse. Against its own 10 m scale bar, the back wall of the U is drawn 30 m long and the side arms add about 7 m each, so the cabinets total about 44 m: the real room was about 15 m and the real cabinets about 30 m. The caption's 'the hall is some two thousand times longer than the chip' only works for the 30 m run of cabinets. With a die of about 13 mm (M4 about 166 mm²), a 15 m room is about 1,150 times the chip.
fix: Redraw the U with a back wall of about 15 m (1.5 scale bars) and about 30 m of cabinets in total. Description: "a U of cabinets, nearly thirty metres of them, around a fifteen-metre room". Caption: "ENIAC's 17,468 vacuum tubes filled nearly thirty metres of cabinets; the M4 fits under a fingertip and holds 28 billion transistors, about 1.6 million times as many switches. Each is drawn at its own scale: in life ENIAC's cabinets run some two thousand times longer than the chip." Sources: as for p1; the M4 die is 165.9 mm² per the MyDrivers die shot (wccftech.com/snapdragon-x-elite-die-shot-compared-with-apple-m4).
reason: Seen in the screenshot: against the 10 m bar (about 215 px) the back wall is about 644 px (30 m) and each arm about 170 px (8 m), so the drawn cabinets total about 46 m, about 1.5 times the real 30 m. The caption's 'hall ... two thousand times longer' only holds for the 30 m run. Same root as finding 1 but it needs a separate redraw.
judge_fix: Redraw so the whole U (back wall plus both arms) measures 30 m against the 10 m bar: shorten the U, or lengthen the bar to about 330 px and scale the person to match (about 56 px). Description and docs/pass-30-figures.md row: "a U of cabinets, thirty metres of them in all". Caption (ch1-transistor-p17): "ENIAC's 17,468 vacuum tubes filled thirty metres of cabinets; the M4 fits under a fingertip and holds 28 billion transistors, about 1.6 million times as many switches. Each is drawn at its own scale: in life ENIAC's cabinets run some two thousand times longer than the chip." (30 m over a die of about 13 mm is about 2,300.)

quote: In the transistor the control goes to the base of a small piece of silicon
problem: The figure dates the device 'TRANSISTOR 1947' and labels its body 'silicon'. The 1947 Bell Labs point-contact transistor was germanium, and every transistor stayed germanium until Tanenbaum's silicon transistor in January 1954. The book itself says germanium came first (p9 on Kilby, the p13 timeline), so the figure contradicts the prose.
fix: Change the drawn word 'silicon' to 'germanium', and in the description write 'a small piece of germanium'. Make the caption's second sentence: "The transistor does it in a sliver of semiconductor (germanium in 1947, silicon today), with no glass, no glowing filament and nothing to burn out." Source: computerhistory.org/siliconengine/silicon-transistors-offer-superior-operating-characteristics/ ("For the first six years of their existence, transistors had all been made with germanium").
reason: Screenshot shows 'TRANSISTOR 1947' with the drawn word 'silicon'. The 1947 Bardeen-Brattain device was a germanium crystal (Wikipedia Transistor); silicon transistors came in 1954. The book itself calls germanium Kilby's material in p9 and says silicon won in the timeline, so the figure contradicts the prose.
judge_fix: Use 'semiconductor' in place of the drawn word 'silicon' (it is defined in p7, and this avoids dating the device wrongly). Description: 'the control goes to the base of a small piece of semiconductor'. Caption (ch1-transistor-p3), second sentence: "The transistor does it in a sliver of semiconductor crystal, with no glass, no glowing filament and nothing to burn out." Strip 'Transistor': "...current flows through the semiconductor between the other two terminals...". Update the docs/pass-30-figures.md row 'small piece of silicon'. Keep p7's silicon explanation, since it is about modern chips.

quote: pulls electrons (blue dots) up into a thin channel under it
problem: With the gate off, the drawing puts nine free electrons in the p-type body and none in the two n-type regions. When the gate turns on, the channel fills with electrons rising out of that body. This gets the doping backwards. The strip says n-type is 'rich in free electrons' and p-type is electron-accepting, and p7 says the gate 'draws free electrons out of the source and drain'. In a real MOSFET the channel electrons come from the source and drain, because the p-type body has almost none. The cold reader stumbled on exactly this point in Pass 29.
fix: In the resting frame, put the free electrons inside the two n-type regions and at most one or two in the p-type body. When the gate turns on, animate them flowing in from the source and drain to fill the channel. Description: "A positive gate voltage acts through the oxide as a field and draws electrons (blue dots) out of the source and drain into a thin channel under it; they flow along it from source to drain."
reason: Screenshots: with the gate off, nine free electrons sit in the p-type body and only one in the n-type regions; when the gate is on they rise into the channel. That reverses the doping story in p7 and the strip (n-type rich in electrons, the gate draws electrons out of the source and drain). The caption also says electrons are pulled 'up', so a careful reader will stop here.
judge_fix: Redraw the resting frame with the free electrons inside the source and drain n-type regions (one or two stray ones at most in the p-type body); when the gate goes on, animate them moving in from both ends to fill the channel. Description: "A positive gate voltage acts through the oxide as a field and draws electrons (blue dots) out of the source and drain into a thin channel under it; they flow along it from source to drain." Caption (ch1-transistor-p8) first sentence: "A positive voltage on the gate draws electrons in from the source and drain until they form a thin channel under the oxide, and current flows."

quote: formed in one piece of germanium (another semiconductor) instead of made separately and wired by hand
problem: Kilby's 1958 parts were formed in one piece of germanium, but they were still connected by hand-bonded gold wires. Putting the wiring on the chip itself (aluminium laid over the oxide) was Noyce's planar step, and it is exactly why his process was 'more manufacturable'. Noyce's 'within months' was his notebook concept of 23 January 1959; the first working planar IC was tested on 27 September 1960. The glossary entry for 'integrated circuit' repeats 'within months'.
fix: "...formed in one piece of germanium (another semiconductor), though its parts were still joined by hand with fine gold wires. Within months, Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor independently conceived the same on silicon, with the wiring laid on the chip itself, and his more manufacturable process became the basis of the entire industry." Update the glossary to match. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invention_of_the_integrated_circuit ("connected by gold wires"; Noyce 23 January 1959; first operational device 27 September 1960; aluminium metallization).
reason: Kilby's 1958 parts were formed in one piece of germanium but were still connected by hand-bonded gold wires; putting the wiring on the chip was Noyce's planar step, which is the reason his process was more manufacturable (Wikipedia Invention_of_the_integrated_circuit). The sentence as written hides that. 'Within months' is true of Noyce's January 1959 concept, not a working device (27 Sept 1960). This is also the p9 owner call left from Pass 29 (docs/pass-29-owner-calls.md line 166). Findings 17 is folded in here.
judge_fix: ch1-transistor-p9: "In 1958, Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments made the first **integrated circuit**: a transistor and the other parts of a small circuit, formed in one piece of germanium (another semiconductor), though still joined by hand with fine wires. Within months, Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor conceived the same on silicon with the wiring laid on the chip itself, and his more manufacturable process became the basis of the entire industry." Glossary 'integrated circuit': "...first by Jack Kilby in germanium in 1958 and, within months, by Robert Noyce's silicon design, with the wiring on the chip."

quote: This is roughly what C's "int x = 5 + 3;" compiles to
problem: The comment in the code block after p5 is false. Compilers fold constant expressions even with optimisation off: clang -O0 compiles `int x = 5 + 3;` to the single instruction `mov dword ptr [rbp - 4], 8` (checked locally). No compiler emits mov 5, mov 3, add for this line.
fix: Replace the comment line with "; Adding 5 and 3 in registers, one step at a time". Or keep the C reference and say "; Roughly what C's "x = a + b;" becomes once a and b hold 5 and 3".
reason: Compilers fold constant expressions even at -O0, so `int x = 5 + 3;` never becomes mov 5, mov 3, add. 'Roughly' does not cover a different sequence. Easy to catch for any reader who tries godbolt. Findings 23 is folded in here.
judge_fix: Replace the comment line with: "; The steps behind an addition like C's \"a + b\", with a = 5 and b = 3 held in registers". Keep the rest of the block.

quote: They called it the transistor, a contraction of transfer resistor.
problem: Bardeen and Brattain did not name it. Their Bell Labs colleague John R. Pierce coined 'transistor', and staff chose it from a list of candidates by ballot in May 1948.
fix: "Bell Labs named it the transistor, a contraction of transfer resistor." Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Pierce; pbs.org/transistor/album1/pierce/naming.html.
reason: John R. Pierce coined the name and Bell Labs staff chose it by ballot (Wikipedia Transistor: Pierce coined the term). Bardeen and Brattain did not name it. Low severity, cheap one-clause fix.
judge_fix: ch1-transistor-p2: "Bell Labs named it the **transistor**, a contraction of _transfer resistor_."

quote: ENIAC's 17,468 tubes failed about every two days
problem: As written, the strip says all 17,468 tubes failed every two days. The source figure (and this book's p1 and Fig 1.7 strip) is one tube about every two days.
fix: "A tube is hot, fragile and wears out: one of ENIAC's 17,468 tubes failed about every two days."
reason: As written the strip says all 17,468 tubes failed every two days. Prose p1 and the Fig 1.7 strip mean one tube about every two days. Low, but the literal reading is wrong.
judge_fix: Fig 1.3 strip 'Why it won': "A tube is hot, fragile and wears out: one of ENIAC's 17,468 tubes failed about every two days."

quote: L3 Cache | On the CPU package | 8–64 MB
problem: Next to L1 and L2 'On the CPU die', the table makes L3 look like it sits off the die. In current Intel, AMD (on each core chiplet) and Apple chips the L3 or last-level cache is on the die, shared by the cores.
fix: Change the L3 Location cell to "On the CPU die, shared by the cores".
reason: In current Intel, AMD (on each core chiplet) and Apple chips the L3 is on the die, shared by the cores. 'On the CPU package' beside 'On the CPU die' for L1/L2 suggests it is off-die. Technically true but misleading. Findings 26 is folded in here.
judge_fix: Table, L3 Location cell: "On the CPU die, shared by cores".

quote: L2 Cache | On the CPU die | 256 KB – 1 MB
problem: This range is out of date for a 2026 'typical' value. Current cores carry 1 to 3 MB of L2 each (AMD Zen 4/5: 1 MB; Intel Raptor Cove: 2 MB; Lion Cove: 2.5 MB), and Apple M-series clusters share 16 MB.
fix: Change the L2 Typical size cell to "512 KB – 3 MB".
reason: Current cores carry 1 MB (AMD Zen 4/5) to 2 MB (Intel Raptor Cove) or more per core, so the table's top of 1 MB is below mainstream hardware in 2026, and a reader who opens their CPU spec page will see it. Cheap cell change.
judge_fix: Table, L2 Typical size cell: "512 KB – 3 MB" (Zen 4/5 1 MB, Raptor Cove 2 MB, Lion Cove 2.5 MB; check against the vendors' spec pages when applying).

problem: ch1-transistor-p1 'It filled a room thirty metres long', Fig 1.7 picture 'a U of cabinets around a thirty-metre hall', caption ch1-transistor-p17 'ENIAC filled a thirty-metre hall' and 'in life the hall is some two thousand times longer than the chip': 30 m (100 ft) is the length of the machine, its 40 panels counted end to end (Wikipedia ENIAC: '100 ft (30 m) long'). The room was about 30 x 50 ft, roughly 9 x 15 m, with the panels in a U about 80 ft along the front (Penn Engineering history page, https://www.seas.upenn.edu/about/history-heritage/eniac/). With the 10 m scale bar, the drawing's U is 30 m across its top alone, so ENIAC is drawn about 1.5 to 2 times too large. The hall-to-chip ratio is about 1,200x if the room is meant; about 2,000x holds only for the 30 m machine length. Not in §4g. Smallest fix: 'It was thirty metres long' (p1), with the figure text following.
reason: Same defect as findings 1 and 2: 30 m is the length of the cabinets, the room was about 9 by 15 m (ethw.org Milestone; PBS). Verified in the screenshot that the drawn U is about 46 m against its own bar.
judge_fix: No separate change: apply the fixes at n=1 (p1 wording) and n=2 (Fig 1.7 drawing, description, caption).

problem: ch1-transistor-p9 'Within months, Robert Noyce ... independently did the same on silicon': Noyce had the monolithic planar idea in January 1959 (patent filed July 1959). Fairchild's first working planar IC came in 1960. 'Within months' is true of the idea, not of a working device. Low.
reason: Same defect as finding 5: 'within months' holds for Noyce's January 1959 concept, not a working device.
judge_fix: Apply the wording at n=5 ('conceived the same on silicon'); no separate change.

problem: ch1-cpu code block: '; This is roughly what C's "int x = 5 + 3;" compiles to' is not right. C compilers fold a constant expression even with no optimisation (gcc -O0 emits a single store of 8), so no compiler produces mov 5 / mov 3 / add for it. 'roughly' does not cover a different instruction sequence. Something like 'what C's "x = a + b;" compiles to, with a = 5 and b = 3 in registers' would be accurate. Low severity.
reason: Duplicate of finding 6; same false code comment.
judge_fix: Apply the fix at n=6; no separate change.

problem: Table row 'L3 Cache | On the CPU package' (with L1/L2 'On the CPU die') suggests L3 sits off the die. In nearly all current desktop and laptop CPUs, L3 is on the same die as the cores (on AMD, the core chiplet). Older systems had off-chip L3.
reason: Duplicate of finding 10; L3 is on the die in current chips.
judge_fix: Apply the fix at n=10; no separate change.

quote: no current flows until a voltage on the gate, which rests on a thin insulating oxide over the p-type silicon
problem: "the gate" arrives as if the reader already knows it. The prose so far has named only the base, collector and emitter (p4). The only place that says what a gate is, the Fig 1.4 strip, is closed by default. The sentence is also a read-twice: a relative clause separates "a voltage on the gate" from its verb "draws", and it ends on "under it", which the reader has to trace back to the gate.
fix: Split after "nothing free to move": "...leave a thin barrier with nothing free to move, so no current flows. Over the p-type silicon, on a thin insulating oxide, sits the third terminal, the gate, which does the base's job; a voltage on it draws free electrons out of the source and drain and under the gate, where they form a bridge (Fig 1.5)."
reason: Real. 'the gate' arrives in p7 undefined. p4 named only base, collector and emitter, and the only definition sits in the closed Fig 1.4 strip. The sentence also separates 'a voltage on the gate' from its verb 'draws' by a relative clause, and 'under it' is ambiguous.
judge_fix: Split after 'nothing free to move': '...leave a thin barrier with nothing free to move, so no current flows. Over the p-type silicon, on a thin insulating oxide, sits the third terminal, the gate, which does the base's job: a voltage on it draws free electrons out of the source and drain and in under the gate, where they form a bridge (Fig 1.5).' Keep the last sentence about sand unchanged.

quote: In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the base is called the gate.
problem: Wrong word, and this strip is the only place that introduces the gate. A field-effect transistor has no base. Its gate is a different part that does the same job, through an insulator (Fig 1.5). Read literally, the sentence says the same part was renamed, which Fig 1.5 then contradicts.
fix: "In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the control terminal is called the gate (Fig 1.5)."
reason: A field-effect transistor has no base. The gate is a different part that does the base's job through an insulator (Fig 1.5), so 'the base is called the gate' reads as a rename. Fig 1.4's strip is the only place that names the gate.
judge_fix: Fig 1.4 strip, 'The threshold': '...below it, almost nothing flows. In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the control terminal is called the gate (Fig 1.5).'

quote: It filled a room thirty metres long, weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts
problem: Factual. Thirty metres (100 ft) is the length of ENIAC's cabinets laid end to end. They stood in a U along three walls of a room about 9 by 15 metres (30 by 50 ft). Fig 1.7 repeats the error: its caption and desc say "a thirty-metre hall", it draws one side of the U about 30 m long against its 10 m bar, and "in life the hall is some two thousand times longer than the chip" rests on a 30 m hall. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ENIAC ("100 ft (30 m) long"); engineering.upenn.edu/about/history-heritage/eniac ("a room 30 by 50 feet", 40 panels in a U); britannica.com/technology/ENIAC (50-by-30-foot basement, panels along three walls).
fix: p1: "Its forty cabinets, some thirty metres of them end to end, lined three walls of a room; it weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts, and broke down..." Fig 1.7 caption: "ENIAC's cabinets ran some thirty metres around its room, holding 17,468 vacuum tubes; ... in life ENIAC's row of cabinets is some two thousand times longer than the chip." Desc and drawing: a U whose three sides together make about 30 m (Pass 30 item). Add a §4g row.
reason: Factual. ENIAC was about 100 ft (30 m) long, as the cabinets stood in a row (Wikipedia ENIAC: '100 ft (30 m) long'). The room was about 30 by 50 ft (Penn Engineering: 'a room 30 by 50 feet'; Britannica: panels along three walls). 'A room thirty metres long' is wrong. Fig 1.7 repeats it: the caption says 'thirty-metre hall', and the drawing is a U about 30 m across against its 10 m bar (120 units = 10 m, U width 360 units). The weight, 150 kW and tube counts check out. Wikipedia gives 'more than 30 short tons', 150 kW, and a failure about every two days.
judge_fix: p1: 'It had thirty metres of cabinets lining the walls of a room, weighed thirty tons, consumed 150 kilowatts, and broke down on average every two days because a tube would burn out.' Fig 1.7 caption: 'ENIAC's thirty metres of cabinets held 17,468 vacuum tubes; the M4 fits under a fingertip and holds 28 billion transistors, about 1.6 million times as many switches. Each is drawn at its own scale: in life ENIAC's row of cabinets is some two thousand times longer than the chip.' Fig 1.7 desc: 'a U of cabinets whose three sides together are thirty metres long'. Drawing: narrow the U so the three sides sum to about 360 units (30 m at 120 units = 10 m), for example width 120 and two sides of 120. Add a §4g row (sources above).

quote: enough such rules, wired together, add numbers, hold them and carry out a program like a Turing machine's
problem: Rules are not wired; circuits are. The chapter never names the circuit that applies such a rule, the logic gate, yet the chapter coda ("What you now understand") says "Transistors ... combine into logic gates", a term Chapter 1 never gives. The pointer "(Chapter 2 builds them)" also promises too much. Chapter 2 builds gates and an adder, but storing bits and running a program are only promised there ("Add memory to hold bits between steps, and gates build the CPU").
fix: "Two switches in a row let current through only when both are on, a rule called AND, and a circuit that applies such a rule is a logic gate. Enough gates, wired together, add numbers, hold them and carry out a program like a Turing machine's (Chapter 2 builds the gates and the adder)."
reason: Partly done already: the pointer now reads 'Chapter 2 builds the gates, and an adder from them', so the over-promise is gone. What remains is real. 'Gate' appears undefined in the pointer, and the chapter coda says 'combine into logic gates', which Chapter 1 never introduces. 'Rules ... wired together' is loose, because circuits are wired, not rules.
judge_fix: p5: 'Off and on can stand for 0 and 1. Two switches in a row let current through only when both are on, a rule called AND, and a circuit that applies such a rule is a logic gate. Enough gates, wired together, add numbers, hold them and carry out a program like a Turing machine's (Chapter 2 builds the gates, and an adder from them).' Note: p7's transistor 'gate' is a different thing. With fix 2 it is introduced as 'the third terminal', which keeps the two apart.

quote: One program had the whole machine: you handed in your cards, the operator ran the jobs one by one
problem: The caption repeats p1, the one-sentence paragraph right above it ("you handed in your stack of punched cards, the machine ran it alone, and you came back later for the printout"), and the strip's "The queue" bullet says it a third time. Only the idle-machine half of the caption is new.
fix: Caption: "Between jobs, while the operator loaded the next deck, the most expensive machine in the building sat idle."
reason: The caption's first sentence repeats p1 directly above it, almost word for word. The strip's 'The queue' says it a third time. Only the idle-machine half is new.
judge_fix: Caption: 'An illustrative hour: your job runs for ten minutes of it, and between jobs, while the operator loaded the next deck, the most expensive machine in the building sat idle.'

quote: At a branch the CPU guesses which way it will go and runs ahead; a right guess keeps the work
problem: The caption's first sentence restates p9's last two sentences almost word for word ("guesses which way it will go and runs ahead ... A right guess keeps the work ...; a wrong one throws it away"). The cache-trace point is then told three times: in the caption, in the strip's "The catch" bullet and in insight strip p11 ("The work is thrown away but the location stays cached").
fix: Caption: "The guessed path runs before the branch is decided. If the guess is wrong its work is thrown away, but the data it loaded stays in the cache: the trace Spectre and Meltdown read." Strip "The catch": "Throwing work away rolls back the registers, not the cache (the insight below shows what that leaks)."
reason: The caption's first clause restates the last two sentences of p9 almost verbatim ('guesses which way it will go and runs ahead; a right guess keeps the work ... a wrong one throws it away'). The cache-trace point then appears in the caption, in the strip's 'The catch' and in insight p11.
judge_fix: Caption: 'The guessed path runs before the branch is decided. If the guess is wrong its work is thrown away, but the data it loaded stays in the cache: the trace Spectre and Meltdown read.' Leave the strip as is.

quote: Every core runs this loop: fetch the instruction the program counter names, decode it, execute it, write back the result
problem: The caption restates all of p2 (the four steps, the counter moving on) and p1's "billions of times a second". It says nothing about what this figure adds, the program in the middle: the counter stepping 0x00, 0x05, 0x08 and the jump back.
fix: "The counter steps from 0x00 to 0x05 to 0x08 as each instruction is written back; the jump at 0x08 sets it back to 0x00, so the program loops."
reason: The caption restates all of p2 (the four steps, the counter moving on) and p1's 'billions of times a second'. The figure's own content, the program with the counter stepping and the jump back, is not mentioned. The program counter values check: mov at 0x00 is 5 bytes, add at 0x05 is 3 bytes, jmp at 0x08.
judge_fix: Caption: 'Follow the program counter: 0x00, then 0x05, then 0x08, where the jump sets it back to 0x00, so the program loops.'

quote: With no voltage on the base, no current flows between collector and emitter; with a small one, it does.
problem: The caption repeats p4, two lines above ("A small voltage on its base ... lets a much larger current flow between ... the collector ... and the emitter; with no voltage there, nothing flows"), and the strip's "Three terminals" bullet repeats it again. The brief's rule is that the prose keeps the explanation and the caption names the picture.
fix: "Left, 0 V on the base: the lamp stays dark. Right, 0.7 V: it lights. This is the older kind of transistor; modern chips are built from the field-effect kind, opened in Fig 1.5."
reason: The caption's first sentence repeats p4 two lines above, and the strip's 'Three terminals' repeats it again. The figure itself (0 V and the dark lamp, 0.7 V and the lit lamp) is not named.
judge_fix: Caption: 'Left, 0 V on the base: the lamp stays dark. Right, 0.7 V: it lights. This is the older kind of transistor; modern chips are built from the field-effect kind, opened in Fig 1.5.'

quote: so a program can ask but never choose where it lands
problem: The strip's "The way in" bullet and p6 say the same thing almost verbatim ("so a program can ask but never pick where it lands"). The caption also explains the system call ("a controlled jump into the kernel in Ring 0, which does the work and returns the result") that p6 then explains in full. "The CPU itself" appears three times: caption, strip ("Enforced in silicon") and p7. Meanwhile p6 depends on the caption for what a ring is.
fix: Strip "The way in": "The dotted path is a system call; the text below follows it." Caption: "The CPU runs each program at a privilege level, or ring: Ring 3 for programs, Ring 0 for the kernel. A program's direct reach for the disk is blocked; its system call is let through."
reason: The strip's 'The way in' ('a program can ask but never choose where it lands') is almost verbatim p6 ('can ask but never pick where it lands'). The caption's definition of a system call ('a controlled jump into the kernel ... returns the result') is then given in full again in p6. The figure's blocked and system-call paths are drawn as dashed red and dotted gold.
judge_fix: Caption: 'The CPU runs each program at a privilege level, or ring: Ring 3 for programs, Ring 0 for the kernel. The red path, a program reaching straight for the disk, is blocked; the gold one, a system call, is let through.' Strip 'The way in': 'The gold path is a system call; the section below follows it. The Bridge at the end of this Part opens the mechanism.'

quote: a running program (to the kernel, a process: on Linux, reading the file /proc/1234/status returns
problem: A read-twice sentence. The subject is a list of four things with a long parenthesis inside it, which itself contains a colon, a second clause and a file path. The verb, "are all read and written", arrives about forty words after the subject starts.
fix: "A file on disk, the keyboard and, in later versions, a network connection or even a running program are all read and written through file descriptors, so once a program holds one, the same read and write calls work on any of them. To the kernel a running program is a process: on Linux, reading the file /proc/1234/status returns process 1234's name and memory use as text." This keeps "process" in p8, its glossary first-use site.
reason: A read-twice sentence. The verb 'are all read and written' arrives about forty words after the subject starts, after a parenthesis containing a colon and a file path.
judge_fix: 'A file on disk, the keyboard and, in later versions, a network connection or even a running program are all read and written through file descriptors, so once a program holds one, the same read and write calls work on any of them. To the kernel a running program is a process: on Linux, reading the file /proc/1234/status returns process 1234's name and memory use as text.' Keep the rest of the paragraph, including the Chapter 5 sentence. 'Process' keeps its first use here.

quote: or leave a file's pages unread until needed; when a program touches a page that is not in RAM
problem: A read-twice sentence. One sentence holds three bolded benefits, and the middle one carries a parenthesis with a semicolon and the whole page-fault mechanism ("the MMU stops it and calls the kernel, which reads the page in, updates the table and lets the program carry on, none the wiser"). By the time "and protection" arrives, the reader has lost the list.
fix: Three sentences: "Page tables give three things. Isolation: ... Flexibility: the kernel can move pages around in RAM, send little-used ones out to disk, or leave a file's pages unread until needed; when a program touches a page that is not in RAM, the MMU stops it and calls the kernel, which reads the page in, updates the table and lets the program carry on, none the wiser. Protection: the page tables also encode permissions for read, write and execute, and the MMU enforces them."
reason: One sentence holds three bolded benefits, and the middle one carries a long parenthesis with a semicolon and the whole page-fault mechanism. The reader loses the list before 'and protection'.
judge_fix: 'Page tables give three things. Isolation: no program can read another's memory, because different programs' page tables point to different physical pages. Flexibility: the kernel can move pages around in RAM, send little-used ones out to disk, or leave a file's pages unread until needed; when a program touches a page that is not in RAM, the MMU stops it and calls the kernel, which reads the page in, updates the table and lets the program carry on, none the wiser. Protection: the page tables also encode permissions for read, write and execute, and the MMU enforces them.'

quote: He called it an a-machine, for automatic machine; we now call it a Turing machine.
problem: "it" points back past the whole proof. The nearest things it could refer to are the decider and "Hilbert's procedure", which p4 has just shown cannot exist. The device "it" means was described at the start of p4.
fix: "He called his imagined device an a-machine, for automatic machine; we now call it a Turing machine."
reason: 'He called it an a-machine' follows the long proof paragraph, which ends on the decider and 'Hilbert's procedure'. 'It' can read as one of those. The device is described at the start of p4.
judge_fix: 'He called his imagined device an a-machine, for automatic machine; we now call it a Turing machine.'

quote: plugboard pairs gave about 158 × 10^18 possible settings, changed daily
problem: The same number appears in two forms. The prose says "more than 158 quintillion", corrected on purpose because the exact count is 158.96 × 10^18 (§4ac). The strip still says "about 158", which rounds the wrong way.
fix: "Rotor order, start positions and plugboard pairs gave more than 158 × 10^18 possible settings, changed daily."
reason: The prose says 'more than 158 quintillion', corrected on purpose because the exact count is 158.96 x 10^18 (§4ac, §4g). The strip says 'about 158 x 10^18', which rounds the wrong way and disagrees.
judge_fix: Fig 1.2 strip, 'The settings': 'Rotor order, start positions and plugboard pairs gave more than 158 × 10^18 possible settings, changed daily.'

quote: They called it the transistor, a contraction of transfer resistor.
problem: Factual. "They" is Bardeen and Brattain, but the name was coined by John R. Pierce at Bell Labs and chosen in an internal vote in May 1948 (britannica.com, John R. Pierce; nap.nationalacademies.org/read/11172/chapter/15).
fix: "Bell Labs called it the transistor, a contraction of transfer resistor."
reason: Factual. 'They' means Bardeen and Brattain, but the name was coined by John R. Pierce and chosen by a vote of Bell Labs staff in May 1948 (Britannica, John R. Pierce; The Register, 2007-12-14, 'ft_transistor').
judge_fix: 'Bell Labs named it the transistor, a contraction of transfer resistor.'

quote: 28 billion transistors. 3-nanometre process. Each transistor smaller than the width of a flu virus.
problem: Clipped fragments, the only timeline item written this way; every other item is a full sentence. "Physical limits are being reached" is vague and passive.
fix: "Apple's M4 holds 28 billion transistors, made on a 3-nanometre process, each smaller than a flu virus; since about 2015 the doubling has slowed as physical limits near." ("3-nanometre" kept as ruled.)
reason: Staccato fragments ('28 billion transistors. 3-nanometre process. Each transistor smaller than...') are the only timeline item written this way, and 'Physical limits are being reached' is vague. The owner is strict about this style. '3-nanometre' stays, since it is owner-ruled.
judge_fix: 'Apple's M4 holds 28 billion transistors on a 3-nanometre process, each smaller than the width of a flu virus. The doubling has slowed since about 2015, as physical limits near.'

quote: Gordon Moore predicts the number of transistors per chip doubles every year (later revised to two years).
problem: This timeline item restates p10, the paragraph just above it, almost word for word ("doubling about every year ... he later revised this to every two years").
fix: Give the item something the prose lacks, or keep the title only: "Moore's Law stated: published in Electronics, April 1965." (Source this before using it.)
reason: The 1965 item restates p10 (doubling every year, later revised to two years) in the paragraph above it, almost word for word. The other items add something new.
judge_fix: 'Moore's article, "Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits", appears in the magazine Electronics in April 1965.' It was published 19 April 1965 in Electronics, vol. 38, no. 8.

quote: the distance between them is the history of the integrated circuit
problem: An aphorism closer in the strip's "The same job" bullet. It sounds weighty but teaches nothing.
fix: "Both machines flip switches according to instructions; the integrated circuit (above) is what shrank them."
reason: 'The distance between them is the history of the integrated circuit' is an aphorism closer that teaches nothing. The finding's replacement has an odd '(above)', so the fix below is a different wording.
judge_fix: Strip, 'The same job': 'Both machines flip switches according to instructions; what changed is the size of the switch, from a glass tube to a speck of silicon.'

quote: The Von Neumann bottleneck
problem: The capitalisation is inconsistent. p2 writes "John von Neumann", yet this sentence-case h3 and the chapter coda ("a design choice (Von Neumann's) that defines what a modern computer is") capitalise "Von" mid-phrase.
fix: "The von Neumann bottleneck"; in the coda, "a design choice (von Neumann's)". The section title and the Fig 1.8 label start with the name, so "Von" can stay there.
reason: The coda is already fixed in the working tree ('von Neumann's'). The sentence-case h3 'The Von Neumann bottleneck' still capitalises 'Von' mid-phrase while the prose writes 'von Neumann'. Cheap and visible in the contents tabs. The section title and the Fig 1.8 label start with the name and can stay.
judge_fix: h3: 'The von Neumann bottleneck'.

quote: Assembly language is a human-readable label for these patterns
problem: Wrong word: a language is not a label. "The mnemonic mov eax, 5" calls the whole instruction a mnemonic (only "mov" is one), and "the assembler" is used without saying what it is (only Fig 1.10's arrow shows it).
fix: "Assembly language gives each pattern a human-readable name, one name per pattern, and a program called an assembler turns the names back into bits: mov eax, 5 assembles to 10111000 00000101 00000000 00000000 00000000 on x86."
reason: 'Language is a human-readable label' is loose. 'The mnemonic mov eax, 5' calls the whole instruction a mnemonic (only 'mov' is one), and 'the assembler' is used in the prose before it is defined (only Fig 1.10's arrow names it).
judge_fix: 'Assembly language gives each pattern a human-readable name, and a program called an assembler translates the names into bits, one for one: mov eax, 5 becomes 10111000 00000101 00000000 00000000 00000000 on x86. We will spend all of Chapter 3 on this.'

quote: They also use out-of-order execution.
problem: "They" refers back to "modern CPUs" in p7, across all of Fig 1.11 (label, caption and strip). The nearest plural is the figure's instructions or stages.
fix: "Modern CPUs also use out-of-order execution."

quote: the machine stood idle in the gaps: the waste time-sharing set out to remove
problem: The strip uses "time-sharing" before p4 defines it. The gaps between decks are also not what time-sharing addressed: p3 and p4 tie it to waiting on I/O and to several users at once.
fix: "The cost. A bug meant new cards and another hour's wait, and the machine stood idle in the gaps."

judge_fix: Strip, 'The cost': 'A bug meant new cards and another hour's wait, and the machine stood idle in the gaps.'

quote: when the data arrives, it reloads them and the first program carries on
problem: "them" can be read as "the data". It means the program counter and registers, which were named only in a parenthesis earlier in the sentence.
fix: "when the data arrives, it reloads that program's counter and registers and the program carries on"

judge_fix: '...when the data arrives, it reloads that program's counter and registers and the program carries on.'

quote: driver | scheduler
problem: Two labels drawn in the kernel layer that Chapter 1 never names. The scheduler is the turn-giver of p4, but the link is not made, and "driver" appears nowhere in the chapter.
fix: Add a strip bullet: "Driver, scheduler. Parts of the kernel: the driver gives a device its orders; the scheduler decides whose turn it is (the turns of the text)."
reason: 'driver' and 'scheduler' are drawn in the kernel box, but neither word appears anywhere in Chapter 1's prose. Only the idea of giving the CPU to another program (p4) matches the scheduler.

quote: 4 cycles (~1 ns)
problem: Two numbers disagree. In the table, registers take "1 cycle (~0.3 ns)" and L1, L2 and L3 take 4, 12 and 40 cycles. Fig 1.15 says "If a register access took one second", then gives L1 3 s, L2 13 s and L3 43 s, because it scales the nanosecond column. A reader comparing them expects 4 s, 12 s and 40 s.
fix: Fig 1.15 labels from the cycle column: L1 4 s, L2 12 s, L3 40 s (RAM's 200 cycles is still 3 min). Or table: L1 "4 cycles (~1.2 ns)", L2 "12 cycles (~3.6 ns)", L3 "40 cycles (~12 ns)".
reason: At the table's own 0.3 ns per cycle, 4, 12 and 40 cycles are about 1.2, 3.6 and 12 ns, not 1, 4 and 13. Fig 1.15 says 'a register access takes one second' (1 cycle) but then labels L1, L2, L3 as 3, 13 and 43 s, scaling the ns column rather than the cycles. This is the same kind of cycle/ns slip already corrected for RAM in Pass 29. The cycle values give RAM 200 s (3 min), SSD about 1.9 days and HDD about 6 months, so the other labels survive.
judge_fix: Fig 1.15 labels: L1 4 s, L2 12 s, L3 40 s (RAM 3 min, SSD 2 days, HDD 6 months unchanged), and the second-read label 'L1 · 3 s' becomes 'L1 · 4 s'; update the desc to match. Table ns column: L1 '~1.2 ns', L2 '~3.6 ns', L3 '~12 ns'. Leave the registers and RAM rows alone.

quote: keeps its buffers, fixed-size blocks for incoming data, in that call's own memory (the stack)
problem: The stack is not one call's own memory: it is shared by all calls, and each call has its own slot on it. The opening also says buffer overflows "pass the MMU's checks" right after p10 says the MMU enforces execute permission, which is exactly DEP, listed below as a defence. Only the write passes.
fix: "The write itself passes the MMU's checks, because it lands in the program's own writable memory. Each call to a function (a reusable piece of the program) keeps its buffers, fixed-size blocks for incoming data, in its own slot on the stack, beside its return address..."
reason: The opening claim is already handled in the text: 'pass the MMU's checks, because they write only into the program's own writable memory'. The second half is a real inexactness, though. The stack is shared by all calls, and each call has its own frame on it, so 'that call's own memory (the stack)' suggests a separate stack per call. A two-word change fixes it.
judge_fix: '...keeps its buffers, fixed-size blocks for incoming data, in its own slot on the stack, beside its return address: the address the CPU jumps back to when the function ends.'

quote: pulls electrons up under the oxide until they form a thin channel between source and drain
problem: In the off state the picture puts nine free electrons in the p-type body and none in the n-type source and drain. With voltage on, it raises those body electrons into the channel. ch1-transistor-p7 has just taught the opposite: p-type silicon has holes and almost no free electrons, the n-type regions are rich in free electrons (the figure's own How it works says so too), and the gate draws electrons out of the source and drain. The figure undoes the doping lesson the prose just gave. The caption ('pulls electrons up') and the desc ('pulls electrons ... up into a thin channel') follow the wrong drawing.
fix: Redraw the states. Off: a few blue electrons sit inside each n-type region and the p-type body has no electrons (optionally a few hollow circles labelled 'hole'). On: electrons slide sideways out of the source and drain into the strip under the oxide, then flow source to drain. Caption: 'A positive voltage on the gate draws electrons in from the source and drain until they form a thin channel under the oxide, and current flows. The gate never touches them: its charge pulls through the insulator, as a rubbed balloon lifts hair, and that influence across a gap, an electric field, names the transistor.' In the desc, change 'pulls electrons (blue dots) up into a thin channel under it' to 'draws electrons (blue dots) from the source and drain into a thin channel under it'.
reason: Checked the SVG and the t5.333 frame. In the off state the blue electrons sit in the p-type body (cy 227 to 284, inside the 'p-type silicon' box). The n-type source and drain are empty. The 'on' state lifts them straight up. ch1-transistor-p7 teaches that p-type has almost no free electrons and that the gate draws them out of the source and drain. The caption, desc and drawing all contradict that. The 'electron' legend dot (40,250) also sits inside the p-type body.
judge_fix: Redraw the dots. Off: 3 or 4 electrons inside each n-type region (source about x 45 to 105, drain about x 295 to 355, y 170 to 200), and none in the p-type body. On: the same dots slide sideways (animate cx as well as cy) into the strip under the oxide (y about 162, x 136 to 264), then the existing source-to-drain stream runs. Move the legend dot out of the p-type box (for example beside 'no path'). Caption (ch1-transistor-p8): 'A positive voltage on the gate draws electrons in from the source and drain until they form a thin channel under the oxide, and current flows. The gate never touches them: its charge pulls through the insulator, as a rubbed balloon lifts hair, and that influence across a gap, an electric field, gives field-effect transistors their name.' Desc: change 'pulls electrons (blue dots) up into a thin channel under it' to 'draws electrons (blue dots) from the source and drain into a thin channel under it'. How it works needs no change; its 'The channel' item stays true.

quote: TRANSISTOR 1947 ... silicon
problem: The picture dates the transistor 1947 and labels its body 'silicon'. The 1947 Bell Labs point-contact transistor was germanium. The first silicon transistor came in 1954 (Teal, Texas Instruments). The chapter itself says the first IC was germanium and that silicon later won over germanium (ch1-transistor-p9, p13), so the figure contradicts the timeline beside it.
fix: Change the drawn label 'silicon' to 'semiconductor' and the desc's 'a small piece of silicon' to 'a small piece of semiconductor'. The caption's 'in a sliver of silicon' can stay, since it describes transistors today. Alternative: keep 'silicon' and drop '1947' from the TRANSISTOR header.
reason: The header pairs 'TRANSISTOR 1947' with the label 'silicon'. The 1947 Bell Labs device was germanium, and the chapter itself says silicon came later (p9, p13). The error is small, but it is a factual slip beside a timeline that corrects it. Note the finding's own fix does not fit: 'semiconductor' is 13 characters at x=324 in a 400-wide viewBox and would clip at the right edge. 'germanium' also overflows.
judge_fix: Change the drawn label (text at x=324,y=236) from 'silicon' to 'crystal' (7 characters, same width). Desc: 'the base of a small piece of silicon' becomes 'the base of a small piece of semiconductor crystal'. How it works, Transistor item: 'current flows through the silicon between the other two terminals' becomes 'current flows through the semiconductor between the other two terminals'. The caption's 'in a sliver of silicon' can stay, because it describes transistors today.

quote: ENIAC filled a thirty-metre hall with 17,468 vacuum tubes
problem: On the drawing's own 10 m bar, the base of the U alone is 30 m and each arm adds about 7.5 m, so the cabinets total about 45 m in a hall 30 m wide. In life ENIAC's 40 panels stood in a U along three walls of a room about 30 × 50 ft (9 × 15 m). The figure of about 30 m (100 ft) is the total length of the cabinets laid end to end, not the length of the room (Smithsonian NMAH object record; ETHW ENIAC milestone: U-shape, about 80 ft across the front). The desc ('around a thirty-metre hall') and ch1-transistor-p1 ('filled a room thirty metres long') repeat the slip.
fix: Redraw the U so its three sides together measure about 30 m on the 10 m bar, for example a base of about 15 m and two arms of about 7.5 m. Caption: 'ENIAC's cabinets ran thirty metres around three walls of a room and held 17,468 vacuum tubes; the M4 fits under a fingertip and holds 28 billion transistors, about 1.6 million times as many switches. Each is drawn at its own scale: in life ENIAC's row of cabinets is some two thousand times longer than the chip.' Desc: 'a U of cabinets thirty metres long in all'. In p1, 'It filled a room thirty metres long' becomes 'Its cabinets, thirty metres of them, lined the walls of a large room'.
reason: On the drawing's own 10 m bar (120 px), the base of the U is 360 px, 30 m. Each arm adds about 8 m, so the cabinets total about 45 m. Wikipedia gives ENIAC as roughly 100 ft (30 m) long overall, as a row of panels along three walls. The Smithsonian record gives a room of about 30 x 50 ft. So '30 m' is the total length of the cabinets, not the length of a room or hall. The desc, the caption and ch1-transistor-p1 all repeat the slip, and the caption's 'two thousand times longer' only holds if 30 m is the cabinet row.
judge_fix: Redraw the U so its path totals 30 m (360 px at 12 px/m, which also keeps the 20 px person at about 1.7 m and the 10 m bar at 120 px). For example a base of 11 cabinets (about 220 px) and arms of 3 cabinets each. Move the three red burn-out flashes onto cabinets that still exist. Caption (ch1-transistor-p17): 'ENIAC's cabinets ran thirty metres around three walls of a room and held 17,468 vacuum tubes; the M4 fits under a fingertip and holds 28 billion transistors, about 1.6 million times as many switches. Each is drawn at its own scale: in life ENIAC's row of cabinets is some two thousand times longer than the chip.' Desc: 'a U of cabinets thirty metres long in all, a person drawn for scale'. p1: replace 'It filled a room thirty metres long, weighed thirty tons' with 'Its cabinets, thirty metres of them, lined the walls of a large room; it weighed thirty tons'. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ENIAC (Components); Smithsonian NMAH ENIAC object record.

problem: The label 'M4 · 28 B' (text-anchor end at x=368) is centred under the 2017 Epyc dot (x=331, on the dashed line). The real M4 dot (x=372) is unlabelled at the right edge. A reader takes the on-line dot for the M4, which hides the point the caption makes: the M4 falls below the line. The label also shows for most of the loop while every dot after the 4004 is hidden, so it floats over empty space.

reason: Checked the SVG and the t5.333 frame. The label 'M4 · 28 B' is anchored at x=368,y=65, directly under the Epyc dot (x=331, on the dashed line). The M4 dot (372,39) has no label, and the label is under another dot. A reader takes the on-line dot for the M4 and misses that the M4 falls below the line, which the caption states.
judge_fix: Put the label next to the M4 dot, clear of the Epyc dot: text-anchor end at x=396, y about 19 (above the M4 dot, which is at y=39). Check the clearance in the render. If it is cramped, keep the current position and add a short leader line from the label to the dot. quote: so in any column every stage is busy with a different instruction
problem: The How it works strip says every stage is busy in any column. The grid shows that only cycle 5 has all five stages busy. Cycles 1 to 4 and 6 to 9 have empty rows, and the animation's own highlight on cycle 3 shows two of them. The caption says it correctly ('once the pipeline is full').

reason: The strip says 'in any column every stage is busy with a different instruction'. The grid has 9 cycles and 5 instructions, so only cycle 5 has all five stages busy. Cycles 1 to 4 and 6 to 9 have empty rows. The caption already says 'once the pipeline is full', so only the strip is wrong.

quote: off
problem: When the control signal is 'off', the tube's half of the control wire dims, but the segment into the transistor's base (path M 299 200 H 236 V 326, stroke #e8d0a2) stays bright cream. The off frame therefore shows the signal still reaching the base, which contradicts 'off' and the dark lamp.

reason: In the off frame (fig-1-3 t4) the segment into the transistor's base (path M 299 200 H 236 V 326, stroke #e8d0a2) is drawn bright cream. The rest of the control loop is dim gold (0.35 and 0.53 alpha). The off frame therefore shows a lit wire reaching the base next to the dark lamp, which contradicts 'off'.

quote: filament, always hot
problem: In the off state the tube contains no electrons at all, although the label says the filament is always hot and the How it works says the grid 'lets them through or holds them back'. The holding back is the switch's job, and it is never shown.

Only the on state is drawn, so the blocking, which is what makes the grid a switch, never appears. This is a small missing step that the picture-carries-it law covers, and the fix is cheap.

quote: In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the base is called the gate.
problem: A field-effect transistor has no base. Its gate is a different structure that does the same job, so 'the base is called the gate' suggests the same part under a new name. It also leaves the reader to map collector and emitter onto the source and drain that p7 introduces without warning.
fix: 'In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the control terminal is the gate, and the current runs between the source and the drain (Fig 1.5).'
reason: 'The base is called the gate' reads as a renaming of the same part. A field-effect transistor has no base. Its gate is a different structure that plays the same role. The line also leaves the reader to meet source and drain in p7 without warning. Law 4 asks for a mechanism and not a slogan, and the repair is no longer than the original.
judge_fix: 'In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the control terminal is the gate, and the current runs between the source and the drain (Fig 1.5).'

quote: yours
problem: As the time cursor sweeps the hour, jobs that have not run yet are dimmed, but 'yours' stays fully lit from the start (frame t2.667, cursor at about 9:14). It reads as if your job had already run before 9:30.
fix: Dim 'yours' like the other future jobs until the cursor reaches 9:30, then light it in its brighter gold. The word 'yours' keeps it identifiable while it is dim.
